# Performance Engineer Agent

You are a performance engineering expert. Identify bottlenecks and rec
response:
<thought>
As performance engineer, I'll analyze the accumulated design (types, CAS pattern, SSE resume, polling) for bottlenecks across DB, memory, I/O, and concurrency — the CAS retry semantics, poll/SSE hybrid load, event buffer memory growth, and list-endpoint query cost are the areas most likely to hide scaling issues.
</thought>

<content>
{"subject": "Flow Step Output", "description": "Performance analysis of the Exaix request/plan API design: bottlenecks and concrete optimizations across DB, memory, I/O, and concurrency", "steps": [{"step": 1, "title": "Database access pattern risks", "description": "`GET /v1/requests` (list) needs a composite index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)` — every list call filters by tenant (mandatory per the architect's scoping rule) plus optional `status`/date range, and sorts by `created_at`; without this composite index the query falls back to a tenant-only index scan plus filesort, which becomes O(n log n) per page as a tenant's request history grows into the tens of thousands. Cursor pagination should encode `(created_at, id)` as the cursor (not raw offset) to keep each page O(log n) via index seek rather than O(offset) via `OFFSET n` — `OFFSET`-based pagination degrades linearly as clients page deeper into history, which is a realistic access pattern for a status-polling UI showing 'load more'. `casTransition` (step 3 of the prior design) executes on every executor event, including intermediate no-op progress ticks if it's reused for those — it must be reserved for state-transition writes only; progress percentage updates should go through a separate, non-transition write path (e.g. `UPDATE requests SET progress = $1 WHERE id = $2`, no status predicate) so high-frequency progress ticks don't contend on the same conditional-update row lock as the comparatively rare terminal-state CAS."}, {"step": 2, "title": "SSE fan-out and connection memory", "description": "Each open `GET /v1/requests/{id}/events` connection is a held server resource (socket + buffered writer); at scale this is the dominant memory cost, not the event payloads themselves. Two specific risks in the design as specified: (1) the `EventBuffer` ring buffer is keyed per-request and sized by a fixed 5-minute TTL — for a system with high request throughput and short-lived requests, this means most buffer slots are allocated and torn down within seconds, so the buffer implementation should use a bounded LRU/TTL cache with eviction rather than per-request unbounded map entries, or buffer memory grows linearly with concurrent+recently-completed request count with no natural cap. (2) `write(event)` in `streamRequestEvents` is shown as a synchronous callback with no backpressure handling — if a slow/stalled client isn't draining its socket, the in-process event emitter will buffer unboundedly in Node's internal write queue; the stream write path must check `response.write()`'s boolean return value and pause the per-request event subscription (or drop-and-resync-later) when the client is not draining, rather than buffering the entire backlog into memory before writing, as the current backlog-replay loop (`for (const evt of backlog) write(evt)`) does unconditionally."}, {"step": 3, "title": "Polling fallback load characteristics", "description": "The `ETag`/`If-None-Match` `304` optimization on `GET /v1/requests/{id}` (from the PM/architect design) avoids response-body serialization cost on unchanged polls, but the request still hits the status store to compute the current ETag — at the suggested `X-Poll-Interval-Ms` cadence this is still one DB read per client per interval. For a large fleet of polling clients on long-running requests, this read load is the real bottleneck, not bandwidth: recommend serving `GET /v1/requests/{id}` reads from a read-through cache (e.g. Redis, TTL matched to `X-Poll-Interval-Ms`) keyed by `(tenant_id, request_id)` and invalidated on every `casTransition`/progress write, so the DB only sees a write once per actual state change instead of a read once per poll tick regardless of change. This also naturally caps DB read QPS independent of client poll fleet size, which the current design has no bound on."}, {"step": 4, "title": "Concurrency correctness of the CAS pattern under load", "description": "The `casTransition` primitive (step 3 of prior design) is correct for the two-writer race the architect identified, but its current signature (`from: RequestStatus[]`) executes as a single `UPDATE ... WHERE status IN (...)` — this is good (avoids read-then-write TOCTOU), but under high step-completion frequency for long plans (many `PlanStep` updates per Request), each step-status write should NOT go through the same row-level CAS as the top-level Request status: writing individual `PlanStep` rows (keyed by `plan_id, step_id`) avoids serializing all step updates through a single contended `requests` row, letting concurrent steps within one plan update independently instead of lock-queueing on one row. Recommend: `PlanStep` status writes target the `plan_steps` table directly (no CAS needed there since each step has a single writer/executor), while only the aggregate `Request.status` and `Request.progress` roll-up use the CAS-guarded `requests` row — this keeps the hot path (per-step updates) off the lock-contended row and reserves CAS overhead for the low-frequency terminal transitions it was designed for."}]}
</content>
